claim: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children.
source: Treatment for medulloblastoma, the most common malignant brain tumor in children, remains limited to surgical resection, radiation, and traditional chemotherapy
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by a citation (Dhall, 2009) in the introduction.

claim: Long-term survival for Shh-type medulloblastoma is as low as 50-60%.
source: with long-term survival as low as 50–60% for Sonic Hedgehog (Shh)-type medulloblastoma
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract providing a specific survival statistic.

claim: Atoh1 is required for Shh-type medulloblastoma development in mice.
source: We have shown that the transcription factor Atonal homologue 1 (Atoh1) is required for Shh-type medulloblastoma development in mice.
evidence: This is stated as a prior finding by the authors in the abstract.

claim: Heterozygosity of Atoh1 reduced tumor occurrence and prolonged survival.
source: Heterozygosity of Atoh1 reduced tumor occurrence and prolonged survival.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by survival curve data in Figure 1a.

claim: Tyrosine 78 of Atoh1 is phosphorylated by a Jak2-mediated pathway only in tumor-initiating cells and in human SHH-type medulloblastoma.
source: We discovered tyrosine 78 of Atoh1 is phosphorylated by a Jak2-mediated pathway only in tumor-initiating cells and in human SHH-type medulloblastoma.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by IP-MS data, western blots, and immunofluorescence in Figures 1b-c and Figure 4e.

claim: Phosphorylation of tyrosine 78 stabilizes Atoh1.
source: Phosphorylation of tyrosine 78 stabilizes Atoh1, increases Atoh1's transcriptional activity, and is independent of canonical Jak2 signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by protein stability assays shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c-d.

claim: Phosphorylation of tyrosine 78 increases Atoh1's transcriptional activity.
source: Phosphorylation of tyrosine 78 stabilizes Atoh1, increases Atoh1's transcriptional activity, and is independent of canonical Jak2 signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by luciferase reporter assays in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b-c.

claim: Tyrosine 78 phosphorylation is independent of canonical Jak2 signaling.
source: Phosphorylation of tyrosine 78 stabilizes Atoh1, increases Atoh1's transcriptional activity, and is independent of canonical Jak2 signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments using inhibitors of STAT, PI3K, and MAPK pathways shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1d-e.

claim: Inhibition of Jak2 impairs tyrosine 78 phosphorylation and tumor growth in vivo.
source: Importantly, inhibition of Jak2 impairs tyrosine 78 phosphorylation and tumor growth in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by shRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4a-c.

claim: Medulloblastoma is thought to originate from rhombic lip-derived precursors that have failed to differentiate into their usual progeny.
source: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant primary brain tumor in children (Dhall, 2009) and is thought to originate from rhombic lip-derived precursors that have failed to differentiate into their usual progeny (Hatten and Roussel, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation (Hatten and Roussel, 2011).

claim: Medulloblastoma can be classified into four major subtypes: WNT, SHH, Group C, and Group D.
source: Molecular studies have allowed us to classify MB into four major subtypes: WNT, sonic hedgehog (SHH), Group C, and Group D (Taylor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation (Taylor et al., 2012).

claim: The cell of origin differs among medulloblastoma subgroups.
source: The cell of origin differs among the subgroups, as does the clinical prognosis (Taylor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation (Taylor et al., 2012).

claim: Clinical prognosis differs among medulloblastoma subgroups.
source: The cell of origin differs among the subgroups, as does the clinical prognosis (Taylor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation (Taylor et al., 2012).

claim: SHH-type tumors arise from precursors of the cerebellar granule neurons.
source: SHH-type tumors arise from precursors of the cerebellar granule neurons and can contain mutations in Smoothened, Patched, or other genes in this pathway (Rimkus et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation (Rimkus et al., 2016).

claim: SHH-type tumors can contain mutations in Smoothened, Patched, or other genes in the SHH pathway.
source: SHH-type tumors arise from precursors of the cerebellar granule neurons and can contain mutations in Smoothened, Patched, or other genes in this pathway (Rimkus et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation (Rimkus et al., 2016).

claim: Atoh1 is crucial for the development of cerebellar granule neurons.
source: Elevated expression of Atoh1, the basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that is crucial for the development of the cerebellar granule neurons (Ben-Arie et al., 1996), can also drive uncontrolled cell proliferation and formation of medulloblastoma (Flora et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation (Ben-Arie et al., 1996).

claim: Elevated expression of Atoh1 can drive uncontrolled cell proliferation and formation of medulloblastoma.
source: Elevated expression of Atoh1, the basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that is crucial for the development of the cerebellar granule neurons (Ben-Arie et al., 1996), can also drive uncontrolled cell proliferation and formation of medulloblastoma (Flora et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation (Flora et al., 2009).

claim: Inhibiting SHH signaling can be foiled by the development of secondary mutations.
source: In addition to attempting to inhibit SHH signaling—a strategy that can be foiled by the development of secondary mutations (Yauch et al., 2009)—we hypothesized that controlling the levels of Atoh1 protein will provide another therapeutic entry point for the treatment SHH-driven medulloblastoma.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation (Yauch et al., 2009).

claim: 23.1% of Nd2::SmoA1Tg mice developed medulloblastoma and succumbed to the disease within 300 days of life.
source: Whereas almost a quarter (23.1%) of Nd2::SmoA1Tg mice developed MB and succumbed to the disease within 300 days of life, fewer than one in ten (6.7%) Nd2::SmoA1Tg mice – heterozygous for Atoh1 (Atoh1+/-, Nd2::SmoA1Tg) – developed signs of disease (Figure 1a, Figure 1—source data 1 for all statistical analysis).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the survival curve in Figure 1a.

claim: 6.7% of Nd2::SmoA1Tg mice heterozygous for Atoh1 developed signs of disease within 300 days.
source: Whereas almost a quarter (23.1%) of Nd2::SmoA1Tg mice developed MB and succumbed to the disease within 300 days of life, fewer than one in ten (6.7%) Nd2::SmoA1Tg mice – heterozygous for Atoh1 (Atoh1+/-, Nd2::SmoA1Tg) – developed signs of disease (Figure 1a, Figure 1—source data 1 for all statistical analysis).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the survival curve in Figure 1a.

claim: Atoh1 heterozygosity dropped the overall tumor incidence by over three-fold.
source: Atoh1 heterozygosity dropped the overall tumor incidence by over three-fold and never reached that of Nd2::SmoA1Tg, Atoh1 wildtype mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results and can be inferred from the survival data in Figure 1a.

claim: Both Nd2::SmoA1Tg Atoh1 wildtype and heterozygous groups expressed the tumorigenic transgene (Nd2::SmoA1) at similar levels.
source: Importantly, while both groups expressed the tumorigenic transgene (Nd2::SmoA1) at similar levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), levels of Gli2, the primary Shh mediator in medulloblastoma and direct target of Atoh1 (Read et al., 2009; Klisch et al., 2011) were reduced in the Atoh1 heterozygous mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Gli2 is the primary Shh mediator in medulloblastoma.
source: Importantly, while both groups expressed the tumorigenic transgene (Nd2::SmoA1) at similar levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), levels of Gli2, the primary Shh mediator in medulloblastoma and direct target of Atoh1 (Read et al., 2009; Klisch et al., 2011) were reduced in the Atoh1 heterozygous mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations (Read et al., 2009; Klisch et al., 2011).

claim: Gli2 is a direct target of Atoh1.
source: Importantly, while both groups expressed the tumorigenic transgene (Nd2::SmoA1) at similar levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), levels of Gli2, the primary Shh mediator in medulloblastoma and direct target of Atoh1 (Read et al., 2009; Klisch et al., 2011) were reduced in the Atoh1 heterozygous mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations (Read et al., 2009; Klisch et al., 2011).

claim: Levels of Gli2 were reduced in Atoh1 heterozygous mice.
source: Importantly, while both groups expressed the tumorigenic transgene (Nd2::SmoA1) at similar levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), levels of Gli2, the primary Shh mediator in medulloblastoma and direct target of Atoh1 (Read et al., 2009; Klisch et al., 2011) were reduced in the Atoh1 heterozygous mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: A 50% reduction in Atoh1 protein level has a direct, positive effect on survival in the medulloblastoma mouse model.
source: Hence, a 50% reduction in Atoh1 protein level has a direct, positive, effect on survival in this medulloblastoma mouse model.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results based on the survival data.

claim: Atoh1 protein dosage is critical for the development of medulloblastoma in mice.
source: This suggests that Atoh1 protein dosage is critical for the development of medulloblastoma in mice.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results based on the dosage experiments.

claim: The regulation of Atoh1 expression during cerebellar development involves Shh signaling.
source: The regulation of Atoh1 expression during the development of the cerebellum is highly complex, involving not only Shh signaling but also other signaling pathways required for proper development, such as BMP and WNT signaling (Butts et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation (Butts et al., 2014).

claim: The regulation of Atoh1 expression during cerebellar development involves BMP signaling.
source: The regulation of Atoh1 expression during the development of the cerebellum is highly complex, involving not only Shh signaling but also other signaling pathways required for proper development, such as BMP and WNT signaling (Butts et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation (Butts et al., 2014).

claim: The regulation of Atoh1 expression during cerebellar development involves WNT signaling.
source: The regulation of Atoh1 expression during the development of the cerebellum is highly complex, involving not only Shh signaling but also other signaling pathways required for proper development, such as BMP and WNT signaling (Butts et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation (Butts et al., 2014).

claim: Atoh1 regulation is transcriptional in nature.
source: While this regulation is transcriptional in nature, another layer of regulation has been reported to influence Atoh1 protein levels: phosphorylation (Forget et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results as established knowledge.

claim: Phosphorylation has been reported to influence Atoh1 protein levels.
source: While this regulation is transcriptional in nature, another layer of regulation has been reported to influence Atoh1 protein levels: phosphorylation (Forget et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation (Forget et al., 2014).

claim: CD15 marks tumor-initiating cells that express Atoh1.
source: Using tumors isolated from Nd2::SmoA1Tg mice, we performed IP-MS on tumor-initiating cells that express Atoh1 [marked by cell surface protein CD15 (Read et al., 2009)] and CD15-negative cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation (Read et al., 2009).

claim: Atoh1 expression in tumor-initiating cells is required to drive secondary tumor formation.
source: We tested the integrity of both cell populations by flank injections of sorted cells in immunosuppressed mice and found that Atoh1 expression in the tumor-initiating cells is required to drive secondary tumor formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the FACS and tumor formation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Tyrosine 78 on Atoh1 is phosphorylated exclusively in tumor-initiating cells.
source: Using Atoh1 IP-MS, we discovered that tyrosine 78 (Y78, Figure 1—source data 2) on Atoh1 is phosphorylated exclusively in tumor-initiating cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by IP-MS data.

claim: Atoh1 Y78 phosphorylation is specific to tumor-initiating cells.
source: We further confirmed these findings in tumorigenic and control tissues from mice and found that Atoh1 Y78 phosphorylation is specific to the tumor-initiating cells (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1c.

claim: Y78 immuno-reactivity was observed mostly in the initiating cell islets of the tumor.
source: Y78 immuno-reactivity was observed mostly in the initiating cell islets of the tumor; neither the Y78-specific phospho-antibody, nor an antibody against CD15, reacted in the normal tissue, even in the presence of strong Atoh1 expression in the external granule layer (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1c.

claim: Neither the Y78-specific phospho-antibody nor an antibody against CD15 reacted in normal tissue, even in the presence of strong Atoh1 expression in the external granule layer.
source: Y78 immuno-reactivity was observed mostly in the initiating cell islets of the tumor; neither the Y78-specific phospho-antibody, nor an antibody against CD15, reacted in the normal tissue, even in the presence of strong Atoh1 expression in the external granule layer (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1c.

claim: Y78 phosphorylation status did not alter the interaction of Atoh1 with its E-protein binding partner.
source: We found that Y78 phosphorylation status did not alter the interaction of Atoh1 with its E-protein binding partner or its nuclear-cytoplasmic localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-IP data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Y78 phosphorylation status did not alter Atoh1's nuclear-cytoplasmic localization.
source: We found that Y78 phosphorylation status did not alter the interaction of Atoh1 with its E-protein binding partner or its nuclear-cytoplasmic localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by fractionation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Y78 phosphorylation dramatically increased Atoh1 protein stability in all three parental cell lines.
source: However, upon doxycycline withdrawal, Y78 phosphorylation dramatically increased Atoh1 protein stability in all three parental lines (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by stability assays in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c-d.

claim: Protein half-life of phospho-mimetic Atoh1 was triple that of wildtype Atoh1.
source: Protein half-life of phospho-mimetic Atoh1 was triple that of wildtype Atoh1 (Figure 2—source data 1), while the RNA stability of the transgenes was comparable (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by half-life calculations from stability data.

claim: The RNA stability of the Atoh1 transgenes was comparable across variants.
source: Protein half-life of phospho-mimetic Atoh1 was triple that of wildtype Atoh1 (Figure 2—source data 1), while the RNA stability of the transgenes was comparable (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA stability data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Overexpression of phospho-mimetic Atoh1 (Y78D) increased Atoh1 transcriptional activity.
source: Overexpression of phospho-mimetic Atoh1 (Y78D), but not the phospho-mutant (Y78F), increased Atoh1 transcriptional activity (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2b–c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by luciferase reporter assays in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b-c.

claim: Overexpression of phospho-mutant Atoh1 (Y78F) did not increase Atoh1 transcriptional activity.
source: Overexpression of phospho-mimetic Atoh1 (Y78D), but not the phospho-mutant (Y78F), increased Atoh1 transcriptional activity (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2b–c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by luciferase reporter assays in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b-c.

claim: The enhanced activity of Atoh1 Y78D resulted in hyper-proliferation.
source: In a proliferation assay using all three parental cell lines, we found that the enhanced activity of Atoh1 Y78D resulted in hyper-proliferation, whereas the phospho-dead Atoh1 resulted in a slight decrease in cell proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2d–f).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by proliferation assays in Figure 2—figure supplement 2d-f.

claim: Phospho-dead Atoh1 resulted in a slight decrease in cell proliferation.
source: In a proliferation assay using all three parental cell lines, we found that the enhanced activity of Atoh1 Y78D resulted in hyper-proliferation, whereas the phospho-dead Atoh1 resulted in a slight decrease in cell proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2d–f).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by proliferation assays in Figure 2—figure supplement 2d-f.

claim: The steady-state levels of the three Atoh1 mutants were similar in the luciferase lysates.
source: While the increase in transcriptional activity could be due to the increased half-life, the steady-state levels of the three Atoh1 mutants were similar in the luciferase lysates (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Tyrosine 78 phosphorylation has two distinct effects: increased Atoh1 stability and increased Atoh1 transcriptional activity.
source: These data argue for two distinct effects of tyrosine 78 phosphorylation: increased Atoh1 stability as well as increased Atoh1 transcriptional activity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results based on the stability and transcriptional activity data.

claim: Overexpression of phospho-mimetic Atoh1 (Y78D) increased tumor weight by roughly 40% in flank xenografts.
source: Expression of wildtype or phospho-dead Atoh1 (Y78F) led to a similar average tumor weight, but overexpression of phospho-mimetic Atoh1 (Y78D) increased tumor weight by roughly 40% (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by xenograft weight data in Figure 2c.

claim: Expression of wildtype or phospho-dead Atoh1 (Y78F) led to similar average tumor weight in flank xenografts.
source: Expression of wildtype or phospho-dead Atoh1 (Y78F) led to a similar average tumor weight, but overexpression of phospho-mimetic Atoh1 (Y78D) increased tumor weight by roughly 40% (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by xenograft weight data in Figure 2c.

claim: Tyrosine 78 phosphorylation increases Atoh1 transcriptional activity, which in turn increases cellular proliferation in vitro and in vivo.
source: These data suggest that tyrosine 78 phosphorylation increases Atoh1 transcriptional activity, which in turn increases cellular proliferation in vitro as well as in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results based on the proliferation and xenograft data.

claim: 637 Atoh1-interacting proteins were recovered from CD15-positive cells.
source: We recovered 637 Atoh1-interacting proteins from CD15-positive cells and 278 interactors from CD15-negative cells (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on IP-MS data.

claim: 278 Atoh1-interacting proteins were recovered from CD15-negative cells.
source: We recovered 637 Atoh1-interacting proteins from CD15-positive cells and 278 interactors from CD15-negative cells (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on IP-MS data.

claim: E-proteins were the strongest interactors present in all pull down assays.
source: As would be expected, E-proteins were the strongest interactors present in all pull down assays, but interestingly only one tyrosine kinase, Janus kinase 2 (Jak2), was present exclusively in tumor-initiating cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on IP-MS data.

claim: Only one tyrosine kinase, Janus kinase 2 (Jak2), was present exclusively in tumor-initiating cells.
source: As would be expected, E-proteins were the strongest interactors present in all pull down assays, but interestingly only one tyrosine kinase, Janus kinase 2 (Jak2), was present exclusively in tumor-initiating cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on IP-MS data.

claim: Jak1 was present in the non-initiating cell population.
source: The Jak2 paralog Jak1 was present in the non-initiating cell population (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on IP-MS data.

claim: Janus kinases typically function in the cytoplasm, downstream of cytokine signaling.
source: The Janus kinases typically function in the cytoplasm, downstream of cytokine signaling, and activate canonical cascades such as signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT), mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK), and/or the phosphotidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)–Akt pathways (Levine et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation (Levine et al., 2007).

claim: Janus kinases activate canonical cascades such as STAT, MAPK, and/or PI3K-Akt pathways.
source: The Janus kinases typically function in the cytoplasm, downstream of cytokine signaling, and activate canonical cascades such as signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT), mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK), and/or the phosphotidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)–Akt pathways (Levine et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation (Levine et al., 2007).

claim: The Jak2V617F gain-of-function mutation is associated with increased proliferation in human myeloproliferative diseases.
source: Although one of the most common gain-of-function mutations in Jak2 (Jak2V617F) is associated with increased proliferation in human myeloproliferative diseases (Levine et al., 2007), Jak2 function in medulloblastoma has not been investigated.
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation (Levine et al., 2007).

claim: Jak2 function in medulloblastoma has not been investigated.
source: Although one of the most common gain-of-function mutations in Jak2 (Jak2V617F) is associated with increased proliferation in human myeloproliferative diseases (Levine et al., 2007), Jak2 function in medulloblastoma has not been investigated.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Only Jak2 displayed a strong interaction with Atoh1 in the BiFC assay.
source: We tested Jak1-3 and Tyrosine Kinase 2 (Tyk2), as well as Protein Tyrosine Kinase 2 (Ptk2) in a bimolecular fluorescence complementation assay (BiFC) for an Atoh1 interaction (Neet and Hunter, 1996). Only Jak2 displayed a strong interaction with Atoh1 as indicated by the shift in GFP signal detected by flow cytometry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by BiFC data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Only Jak2 was able to phosphorylate wildtype Atoh1 (Y78) in a dose dependent manner in vitro.
source: We further investigated whether these kinases were able to phosphorylate Y78 using a luciferase-based kinase assay. Once again, only Jak2 was able to phosphorylate wildtype Atoh1 (Y78) in a dose dependent manner in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by kinase assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The addition of phospho-mutant Atoh1 (Y78F) abolished Jak2-mediated phosphorylation.
source: This phosphorylation was specific to Y78, as the addition of phospho-mutant Atoh1 (Y78F) abolished this effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by kinase assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Both Atoh1 and Jak2 are expressed during cerebellar development.
source: Given that both Atoh1 and Jak2 are expressed during cerebellar development and both are highly overexpressed in MB tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c), we tested whether the Jak2-Atoh1 interaction occurs in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Both Atoh1 and Jak2 are highly overexpressed in medulloblastoma tissue.
source: Given that both Atoh1 and Jak2 are expressed during cerebellar development and both are highly overexpressed in MB tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c), we tested whether the Jak2-Atoh1 interaction occurs in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: A strong interaction between Atoh1 and Jak2 was found in malignant but not normal cerebellar tissue.
source: We immunoprecipitated Atoh1 or Jak2 and found a strong interaction in malignant but not normal cerebellar tissue (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-IP data in Figure 3a.

claim: One-hour treatment with AG490 was sufficient to drastically reduce Jak2 and Atoh1 Y78 phosphorylation.
source: To determine whether Jak2 is a critical kinase phosphorylating tyrosine 78, we isolated Shh-type MB cells and cultured them in the presence or absence of a strong and highly specific Jak2 inhibitor (AG490) (Kobayashi et al., 2015). One-hour treatment with the inhibitor was sufficient to drastically reduce Jak2 and Atoh1 Y78 phosphorylation (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 3b.

claim: Jak2 is activated in Shh-type medulloblastoma.
source: These findings demonstrate that Jak2 is activated in Shh-type MB, where it interacts with Atoh1 and phosphorylates it on tyrosine 78.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results based on the interaction and phosphorylation data.

claim: Jak2 interacts with Atoh1 in Shh-type medulloblastoma.
source: These findings demonstrate that Jak2 is activated in Shh-type MB, where it interacts with Atoh1 and phosphorylates it on tyrosine 78.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results based on the interaction data.

claim: Jak2 phosphorylates Atoh1 on tyrosine 78 in Shh-type medulloblastoma.
source: These findings demonstrate that Jak2 is activated in Shh-type MB, where it interacts with Atoh1 and phosphorylates it on tyrosine 78.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results based on the phosphorylation data.

claim: Co-transfection of Atoh1 and Jak2 dramatically increased Atoh1 activity in all three medulloblastoma cell lines.
source: We examined whether Jak2 influences Atoh1 activity through its canonical downstream cascades by using the Atoh1 transcriptional reporter assay. Co-transfection of Atoh1 and Jak2 dramatically increased Atoh1 activity in all three MB lines (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d–e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by luciferase reporter assays in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1d-e.

claim: Inhibiting Jak2 with AG490 abolished the increase in Atoh1 activity caused by Jak2 co-transfection.
source: Inhibiting Jak2 with AG490 abolished this, but blocking STAT, PI3K or MAPK signaling in this assay had no effect (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d–e), arguing that Jak2 influences Atoh1 directly.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by luciferase reporter assays in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1d-e.

claim: Blocking STAT, PI3K or MAPK signaling had no effect on Jak2-mediated increase in Atoh1 activity.
source: Inhibiting Jak2 with AG490 abolished this, but blocking STAT, PI3K or MAPK signaling in this assay had no effect (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d–e), arguing that Jak2 influences Atoh1 directly.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by luciferase reporter assays in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1d-e.

claim: Jak2 influences Atoh1 directly.
source: Inhibiting Jak2 with AG490 abolished this, but blocking STAT, PI3K or MAPK signaling in this assay had no effect (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d–e), arguing that Jak2 influences Atoh1 directly.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results based on the pathway inhibition experiments.

claim: Jak2 phosphorylates tyrosine 41 on histone H3.
source: Prior studies have argued for non-canonical roles of Jak2, e.g. Jak2 phosphorylates tyrosine 41 on histone H3 (Dawson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation (Dawson et al., 2009).

claim: Most of the genes regulated by Jak2 do not contain the predicted STAT DNA-binding motifs.
source: Moreover, most of the genes regulated by Jak2 do not contain the predicted STAT DNA-binding motifs (Ghoreschi et al., 2009) suggesting the existence of unidentified transcriptional mediators.
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation (Ghoreschi et al., 2009).

claim: Overexpression of Jak2 pheno-copied the transcriptional gain-of-function phenotype of Atoh1 Y78D.
source: Overexpression of Jak2 pheno-copied the transcriptional gain-of-function phenotype of Atoh1 Y78D, increased the stability of wildtype Atoh1 (Y78) to Y78D levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—source data 1) and increased cellular proliferation in vitro, which was blocked by phospho-mutant Atoh1 (Y78F) and the addition of AG490 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by luciferase reporter and stability data.

claim: Overexpression of Jak2 increased the stability of wildtype Atoh1 (Y78) to Y78D levels.
source: Overexpression of Jak2 pheno-copied the transcriptional gain-of-function phenotype of Atoh1 Y78D, increased the stability of wildtype Atoh1 (Y78) to Y78D levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—source data 1) and increased cellular proliferation in vitro, which was blocked by phospho-mutant Atoh1 (Y78F) and the addition of AG490 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by stability data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression of Jak2 increased cellular proliferation in vitro.
source: Overexpression of Jak2 pheno-copied the transcriptional gain-of-function phenotype of Atoh1 Y78D, increased the stability of wildtype Atoh1 (Y78) to Y78D levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—source data 1) and increased cellular proliferation in vitro, which was blocked by phospho-mutant Atoh1 (Y78F) and the addition of AG490 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by proliferation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Jak2-mediated increase in cellular proliferation was blocked by phospho-mutant Atoh1 (Y78F).
source: Overexpression of Jak2 pheno-copied the transcriptional gain-of-function phenotype of Atoh1 Y78D, increased the stability of wildtype Atoh1 (Y78) to Y78D levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—source data 1) and increased cellular proliferation in vitro, which was blocked by phospho-mutant Atoh1 (Y78F) and the addition of AG490 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by proliferation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Jak2-mediated increase in cellular proliferation was blocked by the addition of AG490.
source: Overexpression of Jak2 pheno-copied the transcriptional gain-of-function phenotype of Atoh1 Y78D, increased the stability of wildtype Atoh1 (Y78) to Y78D levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—source data 1) and increased cellular proliferation in vitro, which was blocked by phospho-mutant Atoh1 (Y78F) and the addition of AG490 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by proliferation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both Jak2 shRNA-infected tumors showed dramatically reduced tumor growth compared to control shRNA-infected tumors.
source: We isolated Shh-type medulloblastoma cells, infected them with lentiviral particles harboring Jak2 shRNAs tagged with RFP, and grafted these into mice. Control shRNA-infected tumors grew rapidly, but both Jak2 shRNA-infected tumors showed dramatically reduced tumor growth (Figure 4a), in accordance with their potency to inhibit Jak2 (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by xenograft weight data in Figure 4a.

claim: The decrease in Jak2 resulted in a concomitant decrease in Y78 phosphorylation.
source: The decrease in Jak2 resulted in a concomitant decrease in Y78 phosphorylation (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 4b.

claim: Jak1 did not compensate for the inhibition of Jak2 as it was expressed at similar levels in control and Jak2 inhibited tumors.
source: Moreover, Jak1, a close relative of Jak2, did not compensate for the inhibition of Jak2 as it was expressed at similar levels in control and Jak2 inhibited tumors (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 4b.

claim: Control shRNA-infected tumors revealed large areas of infected cells that expressed Atoh1 and had pockets of tumor-initiating cells that co-localized with phosphorylated Y78.
source: Sections from control shRNA-infected tumors revealed large areas of infected cells (Figure 4c left panel, red) that expressed Atoh1 and had pockets of tumor-initiating cells (CD15-positive, yellow) that co-localized with phosphorylated Y78 (blue).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4c.

claim: Tumors infected with the most potent Jak2 shRNA revealed scattered initiating cell clusters, none of which contained Y78 phosphorylated Atoh1.
source: In contrast, tumors infected with the most potent Jak2 shRNA revealed scattered initiating cell clusters, none of which contained Y78 phosphorylated Atoh1 (Figure 4c, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4c.

claim: Atoh1 is a protein not expressed in the post-natal normal brain.
source: Taken together, here we demonstrate that Atoh1, a protein not expressed in the post-natal normal brain, is expressed specifically in SHH-type medulloblastoma malignancies (Figure 4d), and that tyrosine 78 phosphorylation by Jak2 increases Atoh1 activity and stability, thus augmenting the proliferation of tumor-initiating cells in MB.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Atoh1 is expressed specifically in SHH-type medulloblastoma malignancies.
source: Taken together, here we demonstrate that Atoh1, a protein not expressed in the post-natal normal brain, is expressed specifically in SHH-type medulloblastoma malignancies (Figure 4d), and that tyrosine 78 phosphorylation by Jak2 increases Atoh1 activity and stability, thus augmenting the proliferation of tumor-initiating cells in MB.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by expression data in Figure 4d.

claim: Tyrosine 78 phosphorylation by Jak2 increases Atoh1 activity and stability, thus augmenting the proliferation of tumor-initiating cells in medulloblastoma.
source: Taken together, here we demonstrate that Atoh1, a protein not expressed in the post-natal normal brain, is expressed specifically in SHH-type medulloblastoma malignancies (Figure 4d), and that tyrosine 78 phosphorylation by Jak2 increases Atoh1 activity and stability, thus augmenting the proliferation of tumor-initiating cells in MB.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Targeting Atoh1 by inhibiting its phosphorylation on tyrosine 78 presents a viable avenue for targeting medulloblastoma cells without impinging on healthy brain tissue.
source: Our results suggest that targeting Atoh1 by inhibiting its phosphorylation on tyrosine 78 presents a viable avenue for targeting MB cells without impinging on healthy brain tissue.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Tyrosine 78 of Atoh1 can be detected in protein lysates of human samples of SHH-type medulloblastoma.
source: Moreover, tyrosine 78 of Atoh1 can be detected in protein lysates of human samples of SHH-type medulloblastoma (Figure 4e), further supporting the clinical relevance of these findings.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by western blot data in Figure 4e.

claim: Nd2::SmoA1Tg mice have a constitutively active Shh pathway in all cerebellar granule cells.
source: These mice have a constitutively active Shh pathway in all cerebellar granule cells and spontaneously develop MBs (Hatton et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation (Hatton et al., 2008).

claim: Nd2::SmoA1Tg mice spontaneously develop medulloblastomas.
source: These mice have a constitutively active Shh pathway in all cerebellar granule cells and spontaneously develop MBs (Hatton et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation (Hatton et al., 2008).

claim: DAOY cell line is more 'Shh-like' than other medulloblastoma cell lines.
source: While these cell lines have been used extensively, it has been recently suggested that at least the DAOY cell line is more 'Shh-like' than the others (Higdon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation (Higdon et al., 2017).

claim: Atoh1 is a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor.
source: Elevated expression of Atoh1, the basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that is crucial for the development of the cerebellar granule neurons (Ben-Arie et al., 1996), can also drive uncontrolled cell proliferation and formation of medulloblastoma (Flora et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Inhibiting Jak2-mediated tyrosine 78 phosphorylation could provide a viable therapy for medulloblastoma.
source: Taken together, inhibiting Jak2-mediated tyrosine 78 phosphorylation could provide a viable therapy for medulloblastoma.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion based on the experimental findings.
